catalog_quote: The default position for stress in the noun stem is the final syllable. In bisyllabic and polysyllabic noun stems, the placement of stress is correlated with vowel quality: A stressed syllable has a full vowel, while a vowel in an unstressed syllable can be centralized or even omitted in rapid speech. ... polysyllabic noun ending in a closed syllable, the stress is on the final syllable. This generalization is based on auditory evidence and is supported by the fact that the final closed syllable has a full vowel while an earlier vowel in the stem can be reduced or even deleted (see also Lukas (1970): 19-20 for correlations between stress and vowel quality). In mívìŋ 'door' (mí 'mouth' vì 'room'), the stress is on the final syllable and the vowel of the initial syllable ... ... Giziga tone system, which involves two underlying tones, High and Low. These sections describe the grammatical and lexical functions of tone and posit interactions between tone and other prosodic means, including stress and intonation ... [Lukas 1970] Gisiga sowohl als Matakam zeigen ähnliche Druckverhältnisse. Diese fallen besonders am mehrsilbigen Nomen auf, dessen Endsilbe den Druck zu tragen pflegt.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Giziga is a two-tone language (underlying H and L). Alongside tone, Shay posits word stress whose default position in noun stems is the final syllable; a polysyllabic noun ending in a closed syllable is stressed on that final syllable. Stress is diagnosed auditorily and by vowel quality: the stressed syllable keeps a full vowel while unstressed vowels are centralized or deleted in rapid speech. Lukas 1970 (North Giziga) independently notes that the final syllable of polysyllabic nouns usually carries the stress ('Druck'). Verb stems: only that epenthetic-vowel position depends on the tone and/or stress pattern of the stem; no placement rule for verbs seen.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any snippet seen (a feed query for "Giziga" "secondary stress" returned nothing).
new_statements.exceptions: Placement is stated as a 'default' correlated with vowel quality, not an exceptionless rule; the closed-final-syllable generalization rests on auditory evidence only. Interactions between tone, stress and intonation are said to be described in the tone sections (not seen).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, noun stems (citation forms) in a tone language; verb stems only indirectly. Quote is assembled from two Google Books snippets (spacing/hyphenation of the feed normalised, '[..]' marks the join); no page number could be obtained because Brill and Google Books search-inside are could not be reached by automated download.
new_statements.identity_note: Shay 2021 describes Giziga as one language with two dialects: 'Most of the data in the present work are from the northern dialect' (Maroua, Dogba, Tchere = Glottolog nort3047 North Giziga; hh.bib codes the book 'Mostly Dogba-Maroua = North Giziga [gis]'), while the main consultant Saini Sikoua is 'a native of Muturua, where Southern Giziga is spoken, and now a resident of Maroua' (snippets in nort3047/). Shay, Lukas 1970, Barreteau & Dieu 2000 (94% similarity) and Tourneux & Michielan 2025 all treat North and South Giziga as dialects of one language; Glottolog even places the dialect 'Muturuwa' (mutu1250) under North Giziga. The stress statement is therefore first-hand for Giziga as a whole but strictly attested on Northern-dialect data; no South-Giziga-only (Moutourwa/Midjivin/Rum) description of stress exists in any source found. Lukas 1970 = North Giziga (Dogba).

sources.citation: Tourneux, Henry & Antonio Michielan. 2025. Les relations lexicales entre le giziga – tchadique central – et le fulfulde (Cameroun). Afrika und Übersee 98: 98-135. DOI 10.15460/auue.2025.98.1.332 (CC-BY).
sources.note: Section 2 (pp. 100-103) summarises Giziga consonants/vowels after Shay 2021; p. 103 §2.5: 'Le fulfulde est une langue sans tons, alors que le giziga a deux registres tonals (haut et bas). Nos sources giziga ne notent malheureusement pas les tons, sauf à de très rares exceptions.' Nothing on stress/accent. Its lexical data (Michielan et al. ms. dictionary) rest on René Jaouen's file for giziga-sud (Muturwa); p. 99 treats North and South Giziga as one language (Barreteau & Dieu 2000: 94% similarity).
